curriculum.lesson_evidence: Choreographing means making a dance. Choose a story, such as a growing seed or a journey, and plan the beginning, middle and end. Pick the movements and decide which elements, such as level, speed and energy, will change to show each part. Choose a formation if there is more than one dancer. Choose music or silence that matches the mood. Write a plan with the order of movements and counts. Then check that every choice helps tell the story. Take out movements that do not.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Plan a dance called 'The Snowflake' with a beginning, middle and end. Say which element changes between parts.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: 'Beginning: curled and still at a high level (falling). Middle: slow turns drifting across the floor (floating). End: landing low and still (melting). The speed changes and the level lowers.' Each part matches the story and uses element changes.

WATCH FOR
Thinking that you must include as many movements as possible. A story dance is clearest when every movement has a reason, so choose a few strong ones.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Choreograph a one-minute story dance. Write the title, plan with counts, music choice (or silence) and the elements that change. Mark one movement you may remove if it does not help the story, then rehearse.

Write a short reflection naming one artistic choice you changed and why. Movement or instrument work is optional, adult-supervised and can be described instead.

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
Example: Ana choreographs 'The Seed'. Beginning: curled low and still (seed). Middle: slow rising and stretching (growing), with arms opening as the sun comes out. End: tall, wide and strong with a big held shape (flower). She changes the level from low to high and the energy from heavy to light. A gentle slow piece of music helps the mood.

TRY FIRST
Plan a dance called 'The Snowflake' with a beginning, middle and end. Say which element changes between parts.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: 'Beginning: curled and still at a high level (falling). Middle: slow turns drifting across the floor (floating). End: landing low and still (melting). The speed changes and the level lowers.' Each part matches the story and uses element changes.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner make intentional visual, music, drama or dance choices and name their effect, rather than saying an artwork is simply “nice”. Keep every claim linked to an element or technique.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the elements, techniques or performance choices that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. For movement or instruments, use a clear space, ask an adult to be nearby and stop if anything feels unsafe. You may always describe a choice instead of performing it. One deliberate artistic choice with a named effect is more useful than a longer praise sentence.

teaching.fix: Name the element or technique and its effect, not just decoration.
teaching.guided_attempt: Make or describe one fresh example that uses the same skill and write a short reason for your main choice.
teaching.misconception: Repeating the worked example cannot show transfer to a new artwork or performance.
teaching.model: Choreographing means making a dance. Choose a story, such as a growing seed or a journey, and plan the beginning, middle and end. Pick the movements and decide which elements, such as level, speed and energy, will change to show each part. Choose a formation if there is more than one dancer. Choose music or silence that matches the mood. Write a plan with the order of movements and counts. Then check that every choice helps tell the story. Take out movements that do not. Now choose a different subject or piece to show you can transfer the idea.
teaching.rule: Use the same arts idea in a new artwork, song, drama or dance, not a copy of the example. Review clarity, safety and respectful practice.
